## Larco Museum tour in Lima: a collection of ancient Peruvian art

The [Larco Museum](/peru/place/larco-museum/) in [Lima](/peru/place/lima/) is one of the city's leading places to discover the art of pre-Columbian Peru. Its collections of ceramics, textiles, jewelry and other objects reveal the customs of societies that existed before the Inca Empire.

We offer a museum excursion **for $50 per person**. This is the price of our excursion, not the museum's published standard admission fee in Peruvian soles. Buying an admission ticket independently and taking part in an organized excursion are different options.

## Collections worth seeing

According to the museum's official website, its collection comprises approximately **45,000 objects** of ancient Peruvian art. The permanent exhibition spans roughly 5,000 years of history, showing both the continuity and the differences between cultural traditions.

Moche ceramics are particularly fascinating: figurative vessels and expressive portrait vessels offer insights into mythology, craftsmanship and everyday life on Peru's ancient coast. The displays also include gold and silver objects, textiles and ritual artifacts from other cultures.

The museum's visible storage is separate from the main exhibition. Visitors can walk past rows of cataloged ceramic objects. The museum's official information describes around **30,000 ceramic pieces** in these publicly accessible storerooms.

A separate gallery is dedicated to erotic art from ancient Peru. These exhibits reflect the cultural and religious beliefs of pre-Columbian societies. Families traveling with children may wish to decide in advance whether to visit this section; it is only one part of a museum with many other collections.

## Why visit the museum before Machu Picchu?

On a first trip to Peru, travelers often focus on the Incas and [Machu Picchu](/peru/place/machu-picchu/). Yet the region's history stretches back much further. The Larco collections trace the development of crafts, mythology, art and social traditions over thousands of years.

They add another dimension to the archaeological sites of the Andes: visitors come to understand that Inca civilization inherited a rich cultural world. Exploring the museum cannot replace a visit to Cusco or Machu Picchu, but it provides valuable historical context.

A country itinerary can conveniently combine [time in Lima](/peru/place/lima/) with [tours of Peru](/peru/tour/) that include Cusco and archaeological landmarks.

## Where the museum is and how to plan a visit

The museum is in the Pueblo Libre district, in an eighteenth-century colonial mansion with a garden. Its official address is Avenida Simón Bolívar 1515; visitors enter from Navarra Street.

The building, courtyards and green spaces make the visit enjoyable beyond the exhibition galleries. There is a café-restaurant on site, but **a meal at the café is not listed as an included service** on the Ada Tours excursion. Dining and any additional orders are separate.

The museum publishes its current opening hours, ticket information and guided-tour services on its own website. If you require a specific language or access to special exhibition areas, confirm these details before booking. We will agree separately on the duration of the visit and the museum services included.

## What to look for in the display cases

| Collection | What to look for |
|---|---|
| Ceramics | Depictions of people, animals and mythological scenes |
| Metals | Jewelry and ritual objects |
| Textiles | Techniques and patterns of ancient cultures |
| Storage galleries | Extensive collections of ancient pottery |

To get the most out of the museum, choose a few themes rather than trying to read every label. Archaeology enthusiasts may be particularly interested in Moche vessels and the exhibits about ancient beliefs, while art lovers can focus on textiles, metalwork and ceramic forms.

The museum is a destination in its own right. If you have only a short interval between transfers, discuss how much time you will realistically have in the galleries before adding it to your itinerary.

## Ada Tours excursion price

The [excursion page](/peru/lima/larco-museum-lima-tour/) lists a price of **$50 per person**. No particular type of guiding, transfer, meal or duration should be assumed from that amount: the precise inclusions and exclusions are confirmed when arranging the visit.

Museo Larco separately publishes basic admission prices in local currency. Those prices and ticket categories can differ from the cost of a commercially organized excursion, especially where guiding or transport is involved. When comparing options, establish exactly which activities and services are included in each product.

The museum fits well into a trip focused on [Peruvian culture and history](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/peru/) and offers a meaningful introduction to ancient civilizations before heading into the Andes.

## Frequently asked questions about the Larco Museum

### Where is the Larco Museum located?

It is in the Pueblo Libre district of Lima. The visitor entrance is on Navarra Street; the building's official address is Avenida Simón Bolívar 1515.

### How much does the Ada Tours excursion cost?

Our excursion costs **$50 per person**. Confirm any additional services when booking; this amount should not be confused with a standard museum admission ticket.

### Can I see ancient ceramics and gold?

Yes. Ceramics, precious-metal artifacts, textiles and other works of art make up much of the collection. Storage galleries containing thousands of ceramic objects are also open to visitors.

### Does the museum have a restaurant?

There is a café-restaurant on site. Meals there are not listed as part of the Ada Tours excursion and must be ordered separately.

## Which tours offer a visit to the Larco Museum?

The [Larco Museum](/peru/place/larco-museum/) in [Lima](/peru/place/lima/) is dedicated to the history of Peru's pre-Columbian societies. Its collections include ceramics, textiles, gold and silver objects, and ritual artifacts. The museum is particularly interesting after a journey through Inca sites in the Andes: it also showcases cultures that existed long before the Inca Empire.

Our selection features {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} with the option of adding a [visit to the Larco Museum](/peru/lima/larco-museum-lima-tour/). When choosing, pay attention to **the excursion's actual status**: its appearance among related products does not mean that museum admission and transfers are already included in the main tour price.

## How the museum fits into the “Peru in 8 Days” tour

[“Peru in 8 Days”](/peru/tour/peru-8-days/) links the capital, Lima, with [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/), [Machu Picchu](/peru/place/machu-picchu/) and [Lake Titicaca](/peru/place/puno-and-lake-titicaca/). After exploring the Andes, travelers return to Lima before their international departure. We offer the Larco Museum as an optional excursion during this final stage.

This is an important detail. **The museum visit must be coordinated with your flight time**, transfers and any other planned activities in Lima. An early flight may make a full visit impractical; with a longer free interval, the museum becomes a rewarding continuation of the historical part of the trip.

Our museum excursion costs **$50 per person**. This is the price of that specific product, not a universal museum admission fee, and it does not establish that the visit is included in the basic price of the eight-day trip. Use the table to compare the tour's current prices and duration:

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_peru_8d}}

## What visitors can learn at the museum

The museum was founded in 1926 by archaeologist Rafael Larco Hoyle. Its collection contains approximately 45,000 objects and is housed in an eighteenth-century colonial mansion in Pueblo Libre. Everyday items, ritual artifacts and funerary objects offer a way to trace the history of ancient Peru.

Moche ceramics are a highlight, including portrait vessels and pieces featuring symbolic scenes. The museum also displays textiles, jewelry and metalwork from various cultures. A separate collection of ceramics depicting erotic scenes is well known. The visit therefore complements the architecture of Machu Picchu and Cusco with an entirely different source of knowledge: material culture.

Travelers especially interested in historic places can explore [cultural and historical tours of Peru](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/peru/). More information about the museum itself is available on the [Larco Museum destination page](/peru/place/larco-museum/).

## Larco Museum, Lima sightseeing and the Gold Museum: the differences

Lima offers several distinct historical experiences, and their names can easily be confused.

| Option | Main focus |
|---|---|
| Larco Museum | Archaeology, ceramics and textiles |
| Lima sightseeing tour | The city and its colonial neighborhoods |
| Lima + Gold Museum | The city and metalworking |

**The Larco Museum and the Gold Museum of Peru are different museums.** The Larco Museum is in Pueblo Libre, while the Gold Museum is in Santiago de Surco. The [Lima excursion with the Gold Museum](/peru/lima/lima-city-gold-museum/) has its own itinerary. The fact that both collections contain precious-metal objects does not make one visit interchangeable with the other.

For an introductory look at the capital, a city sightseeing tour is a sensible choice. For a deeper understanding of Peru's cultures after visiting the Andes, choose the Larco Museum. Both experiences can fit into one trip if the schedule allows and they are arranged separately.

## Planning a museum visit before an international flight

Lima is a sprawling city. Travel times between neighborhoods and the airport depend on traffic, while the museum itself takes time to explore. Start by checking your departure time and transfer, then decide how much time remains for the excursion.

On the eight-day tour, check your accommodation in Lima, any luggage arrangements, the departure time and the extra charge for the optional visit. Do not assume that a guide or transport is included solely because the activity is called a “museum visit”: the short product description does not specify these details separately.

Ada Tours can help fit the museum visit into the rest of the journey. Other itineraries through the capital are available in the [Lima tours catalog](/peru/place/lima/tour/).

## Frequently asked questions about tours with the Larco Museum

### Is the Larco Museum included in the basic “Peru in 8 Days” itinerary?

It is listed as a separate optional excursion. Its cost and conditions must be confirmed separately rather than assumed to be included.

### How is the Larco Museum different from the Gold Museum?

The Larco Museum presents a broad history of pre-Columbian art, including ceramics and textiles. The Gold Museum of Peru focuses on its collections of ancient metalwork and weapons.

### Can I visit the museum on my departure day?

Sometimes, if the flight schedule allows. On a specific trip, leave ample time before the international flight and account for the journey to the airport.

### Will the museum still be interesting after Machu Picchu?

Yes. Sites in the Andes introduce visitors to architecture and landscapes, while museum objects reveal the crafts, religion and everyday life of different cultures in ancient Peru.

## Lima's historic center in 5 hours: the Cathedral, Santo Domingo and Casa Aliaga

[Lima](/peru/place/lima/) is known for more than its coastal neighborhoods and contemporary city life. Its historic center preserves colonial architectural ensembles, squares, churches and mansions. UNESCO inscribed the Historic Centre of Lima on the World Heritage List for its architectural and urban significance.

The **5-hour** Ada Tours excursion focuses on three specific sites: [Lima Cathedral](/peru/place/lima-cathedral/), the [Santo Domingo monastery](/peru/place/santo-domingo-lima/) and [Casa Aliaga](/peru/place/casa-aliaga-lima/). Together they allow visitors to compare the public role of the city's principal cathedral, spiritual life in the monastery and domestic life in a private house. This gives a deeper understanding of colonial Lima than a quick look at a long series of façades.

## Lima Cathedral: the city's civic and religious center

[Lima Cathedral](/peru/place/lima-cathedral/) is closely associated with the main square of the historic center and the history of Spanish colonial rule in Peru. Inside, examine the spatial arrangement, side chapels and religious artworks. Their styles reveal how artistic tastes and techniques changed at different stages in the city's development.

The main square and cathedral represent the public face of the colonial capital: this was where the buildings that defined Lima's administrative and ceremonial life were concentrated. Compare the building's façade with its interior before moving into the more secluded setting of the monastery.

## Santo Domingo: courtyards, library and monastic art

At the [Santo Domingo monastery](/peru/place/santo-domingo-lima/), the itinerary introduces visitors to courtyards, an old library and works of art. Unlike the city's broad public squares, these rooms help explain the everyday and educational roles of religious communities during the colonial period.

Observe how the courtyards and passageways connect the different rooms. Such complexes typically combine architecture and decorative details with peaceful internal spaces. Lima's Santo Domingo monastery should not be confused with the monastery of the same name in Cusco, associated with Qorikancha: these are different sites in different cities.

## Casa Aliaga: history through a private residence

[Casa Aliaga](/peru/place/casa-aliaga-lima/) presents the private side of colonial Lima. Its historic rooms, antique furniture and inner courtyards show how a prosperous urban household was arranged, in contrast to the spaces of the cathedral and the monastery.

It is precisely this contrast that makes the three-site itinerary rewarding: the cathedral shows public and religious life, the monastery the inner world of a religious community, and Casa Aliaga the domestic sphere. Look at the transitions between courtyard, rooms and reception spaces, the finishing materials and the surviving furnishings.

## How to organize the five-hour visit

Lima's historic center is best explored as one urban area, but even relatively close landmarks require time for admission, walking between sites and looking at their interiors. **5 hours** is the duration of this particular excursion, not a promise to see the entire historic center or all the museums in the capital.

The visiting order, entrance times and access to individual rooms must be coordinated with each site's opening arrangements on your travel date. Historic churches continue to serve religious communities, so access to certain areas may depend on services, events or restoration work.

Comfortable shoes, water and clothing appropriate for active places of worship will be useful. Photography may be regulated by site administrators in some interiors; check the rules on arrival. Included admission tickets and personal services require separate confirmation and should not be assumed to be part of the package.

## Who will enjoy this excursion?

This five-hour itinerary is particularly interesting for travelers who want to understand Peruvian history through architecture and authentic interiors. It is well suited to a first in-depth introduction to old Lima, as well as to visitors who have already seen the modern neighborhoods and now want to focus on the city's colonial past.

Other cultural journeys are listed in the [Peru tours catalog](/peru/tour/) and the [culture and history travel section](/interests/culture-and-history/). When comparing itineraries, check whether the sites you want are named explicitly: the description “Lima sightseeing tour” alone does not guarantee entry to Casa Aliaga or the monastery's interiors.

## Frequently asked questions about the five-hour Lima excursion

### Which landmarks are included in the five-hour itinerary?

[Lima Cathedral](/peru/place/lima-cathedral/), [Santo Domingo](/peru/place/santo-domingo-lima/) and [Casa Aliaga](/peru/place/casa-aliaga-lima/). These are the three main sites in the itinerary.

### Does the itinerary cover all of historic Lima?

No. Over 5 hours, the excursion concentrates on three landmarks and the surrounding historic center. Other museums and more distant parts of the capital require a different itinerary or additional time.

### Are admission tickets included?

The tickets included in the price must be confirmed when arranging the excursion. Admission conditions and payment for individual sites should be agreed when selecting a date.

### How is Casa Aliaga different from the monastery?

[Casa Aliaga](/peru/place/casa-aliaga-lima/) is a historic private residence; [Santo Domingo](/peru/place/santo-domingo-lima/) is a monastic complex. Visiting both reveals different aspects of life in the colonial city.

### Is this a good first introduction to Lima?

Yes, especially if your main interests are history and architecture. Beaches, modern neighborhoods and food-focused activities would require a different itinerary.

## Lima sightseeing tour and the Gold Museum: planning your visit

[Lima](/peru/place/lima/) reveals many different eras: its pre-Columbian past, its colonial center and its modern neighborhoods beside the Pacific Ocean. The “Lima Sightseeing Tour and Gold Museum” excursion combines a city tour with a collection of Peruvian jewelry and metalwork. It is important to distinguish the **city sightseeing component** from **the visit to a particular museum**. The stops around the city, departure time and scope of the museum visit are agreed for the selected offer.

The Gold Museum of Peru, Museo Oro del Perú, is located in the Santiago de Surco district, in the Monterrico area. It is a separate stop, not a museum on the central square or in the Miraflores neighborhood. When planning, first decide which parts of the city you want to see, then allow time for the transfer to the museum.

## What makes the Gold Museum of Peru interesting?

The core exhibition is a collection of pre-Columbian objects associated with ancient Peruvian metalworking and decorative traditions. The complexity of goldsmithing techniques long before the Spanish conquest is striking: gold ornaments and ritual objects shed light on crafts, status and the beliefs of people from that period.

The museum is associated with the collection of Miguel Mujica Gallo, which originated as a private collection; the museum in Monterrico has operated since 1966. The Weapons of the World Museum is also located here. However, **the presence of both collections does not mean that both are automatically included in an Ada Tours excursion**. If you are interested in the weapons galleries, discuss this when arranging the itinerary.

For travelers interested in Peruvian archaeology, the museum is a useful addition to a visit to [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/) and other historical centers. Objects made by different pre-Columbian cultures should not all be labeled “Inca”: the art of metalworking developed long before the Inca Empire.

## City sightseeing and the museum: how to allocate your time

Lima has several districts separated by substantial drives. The historic center is known for squares and colonial architecture, Miraflores for its coastal cliffs and modern cityscape, while the Gold Museum lies southeast of the main tourist neighborhoods.

The total excursion time is therefore not determined by the museum visit alone. Agree on four things: **the exact list of districts**, the starting point, transport between stops and the time allocated to the museum. During heavy traffic, journeys across Lima can take a substantial part of the day. If you only have a few hours before a flight, discuss which parts of the itinerary you can realistically complete.

If architecture and a general introduction to the city are your priorities, compare the [four-hour Lima city tour](/peru/lima/lima-city-tour-4-hours/). Travelers who prefer archaeological collections and ceramics can consider a separate [excursion to the Larco Museum](/peru/lima/larco-museum-lima-tour/). It is **a different museum and a different excursion product**.

| Priority | What to consider |
|---|---|
| Architecture | Which neighborhoods the sightseeing tour covers |
| Ancient goldsmithing | Time at the Gold Museum |
| Museum archaeology | Comparison with the Larco Museum |
| Short stop in Lima | Travel time and airport arrangements |

## When is it convenient to add this excursion?

In our [“Enchanting Peru + Iquitos”](/peru/tour/peru-iquitos-discovery/) itinerary, optional excursions around Lima are offered during a free day before the international departure. This is an example of how a museum visit can fit between major stages of a journey rather than being squeezed into the arrival day or the flight to Cusco.

It is particularly suitable for travelers who have already seen the major natural sights and want to explore Peruvian history through actual artifacts and city architecture. For families with children, the pace should reflect the time spent in the museum, the child's interests and time on the road.

When enquiring, ask whether admission tickets, guidance inside the museum and transfers from your hotel are included. The excursion's own page does not specify these services individually, so they cannot be assumed to be included without agreement.

## Frequently asked questions about the Lima and Gold Museum excursion

### Are the Gold Museum and Larco Museum the same place?

No. The Gold Museum of Peru is in Santiago de Surco and is particularly known for its collections of precious-metal objects. The [Larco Museum](/peru/lima/larco-museum-lima-tour/) is a separate museum and excursion with its own focus and location.

### Can I combine the historic center and the museum in a few hours?

That depends on the departure point, traffic and the chosen stops. The museum is some distance from the historic center, so a short city sightseeing tour and an unhurried exploration of the exhibition may not fit comfortably into the same time window.

### Is a visit to the Weapons of the World Museum compulsory?

There is no confirmation that its galleries are included in this excursion. If you are interested in the weapons collection, mention it when choosing the program and check the available tickets and visiting time.

### Do I need to purchase a museum ticket separately?

Confirm which admission tickets are included before booking. Ask Ada Tours to specify the final list of inclusions and the time planned for the museum visit.

## How to choose a tour with Lima sightseeing and the Gold Museum

[Lima](/peru/place/lima/) is often the starting and ending point of trips around Peru. Time in the capital can be spent in different ways: recovering after a flight, exploring the historic center, visiting museums or traveling to other coastal landmarks. The separate [“Lima and Gold Museum” excursion](/peru/lima/lima-city-gold-museum/) combines sightseeing with a specific museum stop.

Our selection includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} featuring this excursion. **Visiting Lima on an itinerary does not mean visiting the Gold Museum**, and a link to an excursion does not prove that it has been paid for as part of the tour. Check the selected itinerary and its list of optional activities.

## An eleven-day journey through Peru and the Amazon

The [“Enchanting Peru + Iquitos” tour](/peru/tour/peru-iquitos-discovery/) starts in Lima, then continues through [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/), [Machu Picchu](/peru/place/machu-picchu/) and the [Lake Titicaca area](/peru/place/puno-and-lake-titicaca/) before heading to [Iquitos](/peru/place/iquitos/) in the Amazon. Participants return to Lima at the end, ahead of their international flight.

Day 10 includes free time. Optional activities include a Lima city sightseeing tour and the Gold Museum. This optional excursion costs **$125** within the tour. The amount is the price of the optional excursion on this particular itinerary, not an official museum admission price and not part of the basic cost of the trip.

Other optional activities may also be available during the free day, so it is especially important to consider transport, the duration of excursions and evening rest after the Amazon. The table provides the confirmed terms of the eleven-day tour:

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_source_manyashchij_peru_i_ikitos}}

## What the city sightseeing component can offer

The historic center of Lima includes Plaza Mayor, the Cathedral, the Government Palace and other buildings from the colonial era. A walk shows how Spanish colonial heritage coexists with a large modern city on the Pacific coast. For travelers arriving from Inca sites in the Andes, this offers another perspective on Peru's history.

However, the precise list of stops and the duration of the city tour **have not yet been specified in the excursion conditions**. These landmarks are therefore suggestions to help you choose, not a promise that they are included in the paid excursion. Before traveling, confirm which monuments will actually be visited, where the route starts and whether admission tickets are included.

For a broader choice of activities, see the [Lima excursions catalog](/peru/lima/); for information about the city, visit the [Lima destination page](/peru/place/lima/).

## The Gold Museum of Peru and its collection

The Gold Museum of Peru (*Museo Oro del Perú*) is in Monterrico, in the Santiago de Surco district. Its collection is associated with collector Miguel Mujica Gallo and his interest in pre-Columbian metalworking. It includes gold and silver jewelry, ritual objects and artistic pieces made by various ancient cultures.

A separate affiliated section is known as **“Weapons of the World”**, housing weapons and objects from military history across countries and eras. The museum thus brings together two different collecting traditions: archaeology and the history of weapons.

This is **not the [Larco Museum](/peru/place/larco-museum/)**. The Larco Museum is located in Pueblo Libre and presents a broader view of Peruvian archaeology through ceramics, textiles and the art of ancient cultures. If ancient gold is your main interest, confirm the Gold Museum visit; if you are interested in civilizations and ceramics, consider the [Larco Museum excursion](/peru/lima/larco-museum-lima-tour/).

## Fitting the excursion into the day after returning from Iquitos

The itinerary through the Andes and the Amazon involves substantial changes in climate and several journeys between destinations. After time in Iquitos, it makes sense to leave time in Lima to rest and prepare for the international departure. City traffic can increase transfer times between the museum, hotel and airport.

If the historic center is your main priority, confirm the number of sightseeing stops in advance. If the museum matters most, check how long you will have in the galleries. If you want to do both, you will need an agreed schedule. How much you can enjoy the city and museum depends on the time actually available after traveling.

Ada Tours can help align the additional excursion with the tour itinerary, domestic flights and transfers. For travelers whose main interest is history, see our [cultural and historical tours of Peru](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/peru/).

## Frequently asked questions about tours with the Gold Museum

### Is the Gold Museum included in every trip passing through Lima?

No. The museum visit is a separate excursion. On the [“Enchanting Peru + Iquitos” tour](/peru/tour/peru-iquitos-discovery/), it is listed among the optional activities for a free day.

### How is this museum different from the Larco Museum?

The Gold Museum of Peru focuses on ancient metalworking and has its own weapons collection. The [Larco Museum](/peru/place/larco-museum/) offers a broader introduction to pre-Columbian art, including ceramics and textiles.

### When is it convenient to add a city tour?

In the published eleven-day itinerary, the opportunity arises toward the end of the trip, after the Amazon section and before the international flight. The precise sequence is arranged around flight times.

### What does the $125 price in the itinerary mean?

It is the stated price for the optional Lima sightseeing excursion with the Gold Museum. It is not a universal museum admission price and does not mean the excursion is included in the overall tour price.
